items.title: Americans head to the polls for midterm election referendum on Trump's tenure
items.description: Americans head to the polls Tuesday to vote in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President Donald Trump speaks in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Alex Brandon</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Americans head to the polls Tuesday to vote in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.
items.body:
As Americans head to the polls for midterm elections Tuesday, the outcome could have significant consequences for Canada. CTVNews.ca will have live results, breaking updates, real-time election data and on-the-ground reporting from key battleground states.

DETROIT — Americans are casting their votes Tuesday in U.S. midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s chaotic and controversial second term.

The outcome will decide which party controls Congress and whether there will be a check on Trump’s unprecedented use of executive power over the remainder of his time in office.

“For this country to work at its best, citizens need to be involved,” said 49-year-old Andrew Harris, who cast ballots for Democrats in Birmingham, Mich. “And there’s no better way to be involved than to be a voter — an informed voter. It’s a very important day.”

Republicans have been on defence throughout this turbulent midterm campaign season, with polls showing Trump’s approval plummeting due to rising gas and diesel prices, high inflation and the unpopular war with Iran.

Trump made his closing arguments of the campaign Monday. He defended his administration’s tariffs and policies and claimed his second term has seen the “best” economy ever, despite widespread voter disapproval of his handling of pocketbook issues.

Trump also denigrated Democrats, calling their party extreme and dangerous and claiming they hate America.

Democrats have faced controversies of their own, including a shocking eleventh-hour party fracture in a tight Michigan Senate race. Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

Alan Latham, a 44-year-old attorney and lifelong Michigander, said he was worried about affordability but was more motivated to back a candidate who promises progress instead of polarization.

“For me the candidate that’s going to push forward us in a positive direction as a country, as a people, unify us, is what really brought me out to the polls and what really is important to me as a voter and as a citizen,” Latham said after casting a ballot in White Lake for El-Sayed.

At the same polling station, Mark Pospisil, 43, said he’s pretty neutral on a lot of political issues. Pospisil said he voted for Rogers because the Republican would “honour and fear God and be best to implement good laws for our community.”

Polling shows Democrats are close to taking the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a narrow majority.

Control of the Senate is much less clear and the Michigan race could prove critical to Democrats’ chances of securing the net gain of four seats they need for a majority.

To control the Senate, Democrats likely need to win seats in places like Maine and Alaska, where Trump’s unpopular trade war with Canada has become a ballot box issue.

Trump recently made changes to 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods to offer a reprieve to industries hit hard in Maine, a border state where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough contest.

Polling has shown the main issue for voters is affordability. Many Americans are angered by Trump’s policies which have driven up costs at gas stations and grocery stores.

Trump returned to the White House after promising to boost the economy, reduce inflation and keep the United States out of foreign wars. He made gains among young men, the Hispanic community and Black men based on those pledges.

Halfway through his second term, many of those same voters feel duped.

Dylan Raford supported Trump in 2024 — even though he was too young at the time to vote — and hyped up the president to family and friends. The 19-year-old described himself as a business owner, entrepreneur and “big free market type of guy.” He also works in data centres, which — despite the vocal support of the Trump administration — remain politically toxic for many voters.

Raford said he now feels betrayed. He said he thinks Trump is enriching himself from the presidency and is failing to uphold the dignity of his office.

“I did like Trump. I did. As a Black person, I got so much hate for it,” Raford said.

“He made me a fool. He made all those people right.”

Like many voters who turned out for Trump in 2024, Raford doesn’t really have a party affiliation. He said he’s voting Democrat in the South Carolina midterm races because he wants Trump to face restraints.

The Senate race for Lindsey Graham’s old seat in historically red South Carolina has turned out to be a surprise battleground. Many voters have criticized Trump’s endorsement of Darline Graham Nordone to run for her late brother’s seat, citing her lack of experience and multiple fumbles on the campaign trail.

But a blue wave — which would solidify Trump as a lame duck president — is not guaranteed. Many Republicans remained motivated and organized ahead of the vote.

Jay Jamil, with Chaldean Association Iraqi Catholics in Michigan, said his community was motivated to get out the vote for Rogers because the Republican would be good for local businesses and families.

“Mike Rogers has filled the Chaldean need list. What they asked him for, he helped them,” Jamil said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

With files from The Associated Press

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The new owner of Toys “R” Us Canada will revive the brand by opening dedicated shopping areas within Staples Canada stores.
items.body:
The new owner of Toys “R” Us Canada will revive the brand by opening dedicated shopping areas within Staples Canada stores.

The office supplies retailer announced Tuesday that it has reached a deal with Next Century Ipco Can ULC to bring Toys “R” Us and new Parties “R” Us departments to Staples locations.

The partnership will start with a pilot launching on Nov. 14 at a Staples in Richmond Hill, Ont.

By the end of 2027, the companies hope they will have opened Toys “R” Us and Parties “R” Us locations at roughly 300 Staples stores.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Staples Canada offered no hints about what brands or kinds of toys the new shops within shops will sell but said the new Parties “R” Us Canada concept will stock balloons, seasonal essentials and licensed party products. 

Its partner for the venture is Next Century, an affiliate of Ad Populum, a U.S. firm which owns Party City, manages several toy companies, and is involved with Graceland, the Elvis Presley attraction in Tennessee.

Next Century, bought 150 of Toys “R” Us Canada’s trademarks earlier this year, when the retailer run by Ancaster, Ont.-based entrepreneur Doug Putman filed for creditor protection and put its assets up for sale.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The previous owner said the steps were necessary because it was struggling with inflation, rising labour costs, supply chain disruptions and a shift toward e-commerce that dovetailed with a series of lawsuits filed against the company by landlords and suppliers.

Next Century wound up with the rights to the Geoffrey the Giraffe mascot, the Toys “R” Us Canada jingle and phrases like “wish book,” “gotta get it deals” and “play more ... spend less.”

Meanwhile, a numbered company run by Putman bought 10 store leases, the brand’s inventory, equipment, logistics contracts and bank accounts and balances.

Lawyers representing Putman have said in court documents that he has a license to use the Toys “R” Us name until Jan. 25, 2027, and hopes to extend that agreement or rebrand the business.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items.title: More women in top management, but inequalities persist: UN
items.description: The number of women in top leadership jobs at companies worldwide has risen since 2013, but inequalities remain at lower managerial levels, the International Labour Organization said Tuesday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The symbol of the United Nations is displayed outside the Secretariat Building during an emergency meeting of the UN General Assembly, Monday, Feb. 28, 2022, at the United Nations Headquarters, in New York. (AP Photo/John Minchillo) ]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The number of women in top leadership jobs at companies worldwide has risen since 2013, but inequalities remain at lower managerial levels, the International Labour Organization said Tuesday.
items.body:
The number of women in top leadership jobs at companies worldwide has risen since 2013, but inequalities remain at lower managerial levels, the International Labour Organization said Tuesday.

The share of companies with a female board chair surged from 13.1 per cent in 2013 to 30.9 per cent last year, the United Nations agency said in a report.

The share with a woman chief executive rose from 23.4 per cent to 28.2 per cent in the same period.

But the report found women remain under-represented in the corporate hierarchy overall, holding just 30.5 per cent of managerial positions globally -- up from 24.5 per cent in 2000.

“Gender equality is a fundamental right, and the evidence is clear that it is also a powerful driver of sustainable enterprises and economic growth,” ILO Director-General Gilbert Houngbo said in a statement.

The report was based on a survey of 11,957 companies in 99 countries.

It found a “growing gap” between companies’ commitments on gender equality and implementation on the ground.

While nearly three-quarters of firms had a gender equality and diversity policy or equivalent measure in place in 2025, the share implementing such initiatives -- such as maternity leave and equal pay programs -- fell from 37.4 per cent in 2018 to 26.5 per cent last year, it said.

“At a time when enterprises are competing for skills and talent, leaving women’s potential untapped makes little business sense,” said the ILO’s Maria Paz Anzorreguy.

“The evidence increasingly tells us what works. The priority now is to put it into practice and scale it.”

The report recommended bolstering leadership pipelines for women, using gender metrics and voluntary targets, and improving women’s access to roles where they remain under-represented.

It also called for “action to address structural barriers outside the workplace, including unequal care responsibilities, occupational segregation and persistent social norms”.

items.title: Foodtastic makes takeover offer for MTY Food Group; MTY replaces CEO
items.description: Restaurant franchisor Foodtastic Inc. is making a takeover offer for MTY Food Group Inc. worth about $982 million.

items._ogDesc: Restaurant franchisor Foodtastic Inc. is making a takeover offer for MTY Food Group Inc. worth about $982 million.
items.body:
One of Canada’s most prominent restaurant franchisors wants to gobble up a competitor.

Foodtastic Inc., the Montreal-based company behind 30 brands including Milestones, Freshii, Second Cup and Dunkin’s forthcoming foray into Canada, went public Tuesday with a takeover offer for MTY Food Group Inc. 

MTY, which is also headquartered in Montreal, operates the Thai Express, Manchu Wok, Country Style and Big Smoke Burger banners, among others.

The pitch valued at $982 million came about two weeks after Foodtastic said MTY rebuffed a prior takeover attempt.

MTY said Tuesday that it had given Foodtastic multiple extensions to an exclusivity window to secure financing and close a transaction but said when MTY’s board evaluated the proposals from Foodtastic, it determined the offers were “not in the best interests of the corporation or its shareholders.”

  • Latest updates on company news here

Foodtastic’s latest proposal was publicized within minutes of MTY announcing that Victor Mandel, a member of the company’s board, would immediately replace chief executive Eric Lefebvre in the top job.

MTY offered no reason for the leadership swap, but Mandel said in a statement that his appointment “is an opportunity to establish a new chapter for MTY, grounded in accountability, operational excellence and a clear commitment to delivering value for our shareholders.”

Foodtastic chief executive Peter Mammas said he is making a play for MTY because he long admired the business, but he thinks it has room for improvement.

“MTY is a great company with excellent opportunities, but it has unfortunately not lived up to its full potential in recent years,” he said in a statement Tuesday. 

“We are very excited about the proposed transaction and believe it would not only deliver full and certain value to MTY’s shareholders but also would be an incredible combination for its franchisees and employees.”

David Pullara, a marketing instructor at the Schulich School of Business at York University, thinks MTY would be wise to consider Foodtastic’s pitch.

“MTY has a lot of brands, but most of them aren’t what I would consider to be destination brands. You eat there because you’re hungry and they’re nearby, not necessarily because you’re craving what they’re selling and you’re travelling to get there,” he said in an email. 

“Foodtastic has done a much better of job of brand building and of building craveable brands that diners will seek out.”

MTY launched a strategic review in November 2025, when its stock was under pressure and rising prices, competition and economic volatility were threatening the business. 

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The company warned the process could end in a sale, but when it wrapped up last month, there was no buyer and MTY instead opted to reshape its business, including optimizing its portfolio of brands.

Foodtastic has charged that MTY has “acquired too many concepts — some good and some bad — and it is not generating organic growth in the aggregate.”

“We believe getting MTY’s portfolio back on track requires patient, long-term focus, which is very difficult to do under the short-term pressure of public markets,” Mammas said in a letter to MTY that he published Tuesday.

Foodtastic’s offer is structured as $43 per MTY share in cash — a 32 per cent premium on MTY’s current share price. 

MTY shares closed at $32.75 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Monday.

Foodtastic, which first made a proposal to the MTY board on Oct. 15 and reiterated the plan on Oct. 20, said it was “disappointed” the offer was rejected.

“Nevertheless, we are confident that MTY’s shareholders will recognize the compelling value of our proposed transaction,” Mammas said in his statement.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items.title: Millions of customers of digital bank Ueno on limbo in Paraguay
items.description: Paraguay’s central bank seized a major digital lender with close ties to President Santiago Peña, throwing the savings of millions of customers into limbo.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The headquarters of Ueno bank, a major digital lender stands in Asuncion, Paraguay, after the nation's Central Bank seized it due to its solvency ratio, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Jorge Saenz)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jorge Saenz</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Paraguay’s central bank seized a major digital lender with close ties to President Santiago Peña, throwing the savings of millions of customers into limbo.
items.body:
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay’s central bank seized a major digital lender with close ties to President Santiago Peña on Tuesday, fueling a political crisis and threatening the country’s burgeoning reputation as a regional haven for investors. The takeover left millions of customers’ savings and hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds in limbo.

The central bank’s board voted unanimously late Monday to put Ueno Bank into resolution and hand its management to officials charged with assessing its finances and protecting its assets, the regulator said Tuesday. The move came after Ueno’s solvency ratio, a measure of its capital against its risk-weighted assets, fell below half the legal minimum. Resolution allows regulators to transfer a failing bank’s deposits to other institutions before liquidating its remaining assets.

The bank says it has about 3 million customers, equivalent to roughly 60 per cent of the adult population of the South American country, and manages US$800 million to US$850 million in public money. That includes about US$380 million invested by Paraguay’s state pension and health fund.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Prosecutors ordered the arrest of eight people, including Ueno President Juan Manuel Gustale and chief executive Federico Miguel Vázquez Villasanti, as part of an investigation into suspected breach of trust and other offenses. By Tuesday afternoon, another two bank directors had been taken into custody, prosecutors said.

Peña, who canceled a planned trip to an international summit in Spain late Monday, said that he had asked central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to resign and had agreed with congressional leaders to fast-track legislation expediting payouts to depositors and guaranteeing the return of public money. He vowed to hold whoever was behind the collapse accountable.

“Those responsible will have to answer to the courts, without exceptions or privileges,” he wrote on social media.

Carvallo, who led Ueno’s predecessor before Peña appointed him, said he had already signed his resignation but would stay on to oversee the takeover because “the central bank needs calm to do its job.”

Customers worry about their savings

Locked out of their accounts on the bank’s app, panicked customers gathered outside shuttered branches across the country demanding answers about their savings, as police stood guard.

Activists called for an evening rally outside Congress to demand Peña’s impeachment and an investigation into the bank’s collapse, while an association of pensioners planned a protest outside Peña’s official residence.

“This really tarnishes the country’s name,” said depositor Víctor González, who came to the bank’s headquarters to ask about his savings, only to be told by police that he and others couldn’t even stand outside.

“Apparently, these criminals are protecting the malicious people who caused this financial collapse,” he added, referring to the officers.

Customers could not withdraw or transfer money Tuesday, though most are protected by deposit insurance. A central bank fund guarantees up to 228.3 million Paraguayan guaraníes (US$38,000) per person, enough to fully cover about 97 per cent of Ueno’s depositors, according to preliminary estimates. By law, that money must be paid within 15 days of the takeover, a deadline that can be extended once.

As a first step, the central bank said depositors would soon receive up to 10 million guaraníes (US$1,700), minus any debts they owe Ueno, though it gave no date.

Those with larger balances face more uncertainty. The central bank stopped short of promising them full repayment, saying only that it would seek “the greatest possible protection.”

The state pension fund said pensions would be paid as usual and that it was moving the roughly 32,000 retirees who collect their pensions through Ueno to another bank. It also plans legal action to recover its investment.

A bank under suspicion from the start

Fast-growing Paraguay has courted foreign investors with low taxes, light regulation and a record of economic stability, recently winning its first investment-grade credit ratings, a milestone in Peña’s campaign to turn the landlocked nation into a manufacturing hub.

But Ueno’s collapse revives long-standing concerns about weak institutions. Paraguay ranked 150th of 182 countries and territories in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, tied with Bangladesh and the Central African Republic.

Peña’s own ties to Ueno have fueled some of those concerns since he took office in 2023. Soon after his inauguration, he named Carvallo to run the central bank. Critics called the appointment a conflict of interest, though the regulator has said Carvallo recused himself from decisions involving Ueno.

Peña remained a business partner of Grupo Vázquez, the conglomerate that owns Ueno, until March 2025. He repeatedly dismissed concerns about its finances, accusing the media of fearmongering. Meanwhile, government agencies and state funds poured money into Ueno. The bank said last month that public money accounted for about a quarter of its deposits.

Less than a week ago, Ueno announced plans to raise US$100 million in fresh capital, half from its holding company and half from shares to be sold to local private investors. Fitch Ratings changed its outlook on the bank to negative last month, citing rapid growth in its balance sheet and a high level of intangible assets.

  • Latest updates on currencies here

The central bank said it warned Ueno in June that it was lending too much money to companies tied to its owners. Banks face strict limits on such loans because they let owners funnel customers’ savings into their own businesses.

“There was a great deal of flexibility in financial and banking rules that allowed this institution to expand very rapidly,” said Luis Rojas, a Paraguayan economist. “There was preferential treatment, which raised a lot of suspicions.”

Opposition senators said Tuesday they would seek to impeach Peña over his handling of public money deposited at Ueno. To succeed, they would have to win over lawmakers from his own Colorado Party, which controls both chambers of Congress and has governed Paraguay for all but five years since 1947, including during a lengthy military dictatorship.

Peña, a former International Monetary Fund economist who cast himself as a modernizer of both the country and its entrenched ruling party, cannot seek reelection in 2028. But as factions jockey to succeed him, the crisis has exacerbated political rifts. Rodolfo Friedmann, a party vice president, called for Peña’s expulsion, while Senate President Basilio Núñez defended the president and blamed the central bank instead.

Emilio Sanabria and Isabel Debre, The Associated Press

DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina. Associated Press writer Nayara Batschke in Santiago, Chile, contributed to this report.

items.title: De Havilland to ramp up production after $2.5B in federal financing
items.description: The federal government is pledging up to $2.5 billion in financing for Canadair water bomber maker De Havilland Canada in a bid to ramp up production.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Canadair water bomber provides a steady stream of water to assist crews on the ground at the Paddy's Pond wildfire, just outside St. John's, N.L., on Thursday, Aug. 14, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Daly]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Paul Daly</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal government is pledging up to $2.5 billion in financing for Canadair water bomber maker De Havilland Canada in a bid to ramp up production.
items.body:
The federal government has pledged up to $2.5 billion in financing for Canadair water bomber maker De Havilland Canada in a bid to ramp up production of the iconic firefighting aircraft.

The money will allow for a second assembly line in Alberta, the Finance Department said. And it will provide the means to double production capacity to an eventual 20 water-scooping planes per year, according to De Havilland.

The manufacturer, whose “super scoopers” can suck up more than 6,000 litres of water in 12 seconds and dump it on wildfires, also says it will put the cash toward new staff and production in Victoria, Calgary and Ontario.

The funding is expected to take the form of loans and loan guarantees, delivered by Export Development Canada, said Finance Department spokesperson Benoit Mayrand. The interest rates and repayment terms are confidential.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Demand for amphibious firefighting aircraft is on the rise as the scale and intensity of wildfires increases and the need for tools to fend off climate disasters grows more urgent.

The yellow Canadair turboprops serve as the only aircraft of their kind currently in production built from the outset for that purpose, rather than being retrofitted to douse flames.

However, competition is hot on their tail fin.

Aerospace companies such as Positive Aviation, Kepplair Evolution and Hynaero of France are all developing water bombers. Italy’s 19-01 Holding aims to roll out its first prototype, which can scoop roughly twice the water volume of the DHC-515, by 2028.

De Havilland revived production of the Canadian-made planes in 2022 after several European countries placed orders for the program. The assembly line had halted in 2015, when it was run by Bombardier Inc.

Revving up has been a challenge, and the company has yet to churn out a single aircraft. The years-long hiatus meant a supply chain that drew on 60,000 parts had evaporated. Procurement hurdles have helped push the projected delivery date for the first Canadair DHC-515 (formerly called the CL-515) to early 2028.

Until last week it was sold out through 2034, though the fresh financing will now let more planes be assembled simultaneously starting in 2030, the company said in a release.

Even as it struggles to meet demand from other countries, De Havilland has been calling for a national fleet of water bombers at home.

Neil Sweeney, the company’s vice-president of corporate affairs, said in a recent interview that an order for 50 new water bombers from the federal government or the provinces would give it the financial runway — billions of dollars — to launch a second production line at the assembly plant currently under construction 30 minutes east of Calgary in Wheatland County.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Something comparable to that goal seemed on the cusp of fruition in September, when a draft joint statement from the Canada-European Union summit and seen by The Canadian Press pledged an order for 50 De Havilland water bombers. However, the final joint statement last week stuck with the 24 planes already ordered by European countries, with no fresh batch of orders emerging.

Questions around financial liability and production capacity persist.

“My question is, who carries the risk if there’s an issue with De Havilland being able to build these airplanes at scale,” said John Gradek, who teaches aviation management at McGill University.

“De Havilland’s never built one of these airplanes.”

Industry insiders have also highlighted the pace of production for the water bombers, which will be riveted by hand and roll off the line at a projected rate of 10 per year — 20 eventually — partly due to a lack of automation.

“De Havilland is building this airplane the way Canadair built it in the 1960s,” Gradek said, referring to the Montreal-based company that was nationalized in the 1970s before its purchase by Bombardier in 1986.

Decades later, automation typically plays a much greater role aircraft production, he noted.

“I want to know where this money is going, and I want to make sure that … they’re not just replicating a hand-built or a hand-assembled airplane. That’s not the way we build airplanes in 2026.”

De Havilland did not respond to a request for comment.

However, CEO Brian Chafe has framed the facility now under construction as a “world-class aerospace hub” and a “state-of-the-art campus.”

  • Latest updates on international news here

“De Havilland Canada will use this financing to hire new staff and invest in additional production capacity across its Canadian sites in Victoria, Calgary, Toronto, Kitchener and Fort Erie with supply chain jobs being created from Newfoundland to British Columbia,” it said in a release Friday.

The Finance Department did not lay out any potential reporting requirements.

“Specific commercial terms and conditions, including applicable interest rates and repayment terms, are subject to commercial confidentiality,” Mayrand said.

There are about 160 water bombers currently in service across the globe, mainly in Canada, the United States and Europe.

The 38 new planes now on the order book comprise 24 for six European countries as well as six for Ontario, five for Alberta — for $400 million, or $80 million apiece — and three for Manitoba, according to De Havilland.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items.title: Fiscal and monetary policy are not at odds, Bank of Canada's Macklem tells MPs
items.description: Bank of Canada's Tiff Macklem says he doesn’t think the federal government’s fiscal policy is at odds with the central bank’s efforts to control inflation.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Governor of the Bank of Canada Tiff Macklem prepares to appear before the Standing Committee on Finance on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Bank of Canada's Tiff Macklem says he doesn’t think the federal government’s fiscal policy is at odds with the central bank’s efforts to control inflation.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem told members of Parliament on Tuesday he doesn’t think the federal government’s fiscal policy is at odds with the central bank’s efforts to control inflation.

Macklem and senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers were speaking at the House of Commons finance committee two days before the Liberal government plans to table its 2026 federal budget.

Conservative finance critic Michael Chong asked Macklem for his opinion on the government’s affordability efforts. The central bank governor declined to answer directly.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

He said he only comments on the government’s fiscal policy when spending is approaching unsustainable levels, or when the government’s actions are working against the Bank of Canada’s efforts to tame inflation.

“In the current circumstances, I don’t think either of those criteria are met,” he said.

Macklem was later asked directly if he thought government spending was contributing to inflationary pressures.

“No, not really,” he said.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

The Bank of Canada operates independently of the federal government to steer monetary policy, primarily by setting its benchmark interest rate

The Bank of Canada increased that key rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent last week, reflecting worries about inflation pressures bubbling up from the war in the Middle East.

Macklem did comment publicly on the pace of government spending three years earlier. He warned at the time that spending was adding to demand faster than it was increasing supply and said the trend was “not helpful” for getting inflation back under control.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre regularly rails against the Liberal government over what he calls inflationary spending. He has urged the government to slash spending ahead of Thursday’s budget to help get costs under control.

Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the Liberal government has projected broadly deeper deficits as part of a bid to pivot the economy away from dependence on the United States.

In a press release issued Tuesday about Canadians struggling to afford basic necessities, the Conservatives pinned the blame on Liberal policies and Carney’s fiscal agenda in particular.

“He is spending more on almost everything, passing costs on to Canadians through higher inflation and interest rates,” the release said.

Macklem told MPs on the finance committee Tuesday that the primary force driving inflation higher in Canada right now is the global energy shock from the Middle East war.

The Conservatives are calling on the Liberals to suspend federal taxes and levies on fuel until the summer to ease cost-of-living pressures for Canadians.

Desjardins deputy chief economist Randall Bartlett said in an interview after the Bank of Canada’s rate hike last week that government spending is barely affecting the inflation outlook.

“Federal deficits do support higher inflation than would be otherwise the case, but only to a very, very minor degree,” Bartlett said.

“We don’t think the federal government deficits are inflationary at this point.”

Macklem told MPs on Tuesday that Canada’s economy is in a state of excess supply — an economic term that means Canadian businesses are producing goods and services faster than consumer demand can keep up.

If federal spending includes transfers to Canadians or other levels of government, that can add to demand in the economy. But as long as the economy is in excess supply, those measures would not be expected to significantly add to inflation.

Macklem said it matters what the government is spending its money on — productive investments that add to long-term supply can give the economy more runway to grow without stoking inflation.

Many of the questions during the governors’ committee appearance on Tuesday revolved around a 2024 speech given by Rogers in which she declared Canada was facing a productivity emergency.

She told MPs productivity is a critical metric for Canada because it drives higher wages and improved standards of living. It also gives the economy more of a buffer to absorb shocks without spurring inflation or interest rate hikes.

Rogers said productivity hasn’t improved sharply since her 2024 speech but the central bank does see “some promising indicators.”

Business investment is showing signs of ticking higher, Rogers noted, though she cautioned it will take time before those figures translate into improved productivity.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

items._ogDesc: Organigram Global Inc. has signed a deal to buy Aurora Cannabis Inc. in an agreement that values the company at $561 million, after a hostile offer from Curaleaf was rebuffed earlier this year.
items.body:
TORONTO — Organigram Global Inc. has signed a deal to buy Aurora Cannabis Inc. in an agreement that values the company at $561 million, after a hostile offer from Curaleaf was rebuffed earlier this year.

Organigram CEO James Yamanaka says the transaction is a defining step in the company’s strategy to build a disciplined, global cannabis leader.

“By bringing together Aurora’s established global medical cannabis platform with our Canadian operations and growing international footprint, we are creating a larger, stronger, and more diversified company,” he said in a news release Tuesday.

Under the offer, Aurora shareholders have the option to receive $7.80 per share in cash, 5.8626 Organigram shares per share or a combination. The total cash available is capped at $253.6 million, while the number of shares available under the offer is limited to 205.8 million.

The transaction has received unanimous support from the board of directors at both firms. The companies said the deal represents a 93 per cent premium to Aurora’s share price as of Aug. 10 and a 21 per cent premium to the implied value of the Curaleaf offer, which was amended on Oct. 6.

Aurora executive chair and CEO Miguel Martin says the offer is the result of a robust strategic review process and delivers compelling value.

“Combining with Organigram will accelerate Aurora’s international growth strategy by strengthening commercial execution, expanding our product and (research and development) capabilities, and extending our global operating network,” he said.

The deal comes after Curaleaf Holdings Inc. made a hostile offer for Aurora earlier this year.

Stamford, Conn.-based Curaleaf took its offer directly to shareholders in August after it said Aurora’s board refused to engage in discussions. Aurora said at the time it would consider the offer and was forming a special committee to mull the unsolicited bid.

In September, Aurora urged shareholders to reject the hostile takeover bid, saying it undervalued Aurora and was not in the best interest of shareholders.

Curaleaf sweetened the deal in October, making an offer valued at US$5 per Aurora share, based on Curaleaf’s Oct. 2 closing share price. The proposal included 0.4013 Curaleaf shares plus US$1 cash for each Aurora share.

Curaleaf’s previous offer had included paying Aurora shareholders US$4.00 per share, plus US$0.75 cash for each Aurora share.

Curaleaf did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Organigram and Aurora say the transaction would bring about several benefits.

This includes bringing together complementary operations, including Aurora’s manufacturing capacity, pharmacy and patient network with Organigram’s Canadian recreational brands and European footprint.

The companies said the deal would create more than $50 million in synergies from cross-selling, procurement scale and other factors. The deal would also allow for greater scale and better supply chains.

The deal is expected to close in January 2027 and is subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals as well as permission from the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 3, 2026.

items.title: Why alt lending is no longer the last resort for brokers
items.description: Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians
items.content: <p>Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0000_639293283152242730.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top lenders at MortgageFest Canada say alt lending is now the prime solution for many Canadians
items.body:
The image of alternative lending as a short-term fix for borrowers with damaged credit has, by most measures, run its course.

At MortgageFest Canada, held at Mississauga’s International Centre, senior executives from four of the country’s leading alt lenders made a straightforward argument: the channel has matured into a primary solution for a wide and growing share of the Canadian borrower base, and brokers who continue to treat it as a backup option are forgoing significant business.

“The alternative space is part of your prime option now,” said Cam DelliPizzi, regional sales director at MCAN Financial.

“It’s as simple as that. And if you’re not thinking about it that way, you’re losing opportunity for yourself.”

A borrower profile that no longer fits a single box

The shift is structural, not cyclical. As qualification criteria at Canada’s major chartered banks have narrowed under regulatory pressure, a growing range of creditworthy clients — self-employed borrowers, entrepreneurs, holders of multiple investment properties, and those navigating divorce or Canada Revenue Agency obligations — have landed in the alternative channel not because of damaged credit, but because of how banks define qualifying income.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthONE Bank of Canada, offered a data point that reframes the conversation: the average FICO score among his institution’s alternative borrowers sits at 763. That's a number that, he noted, outperforms some Big Six portfolios in certain segments.

“Banks have very, very specific ways of looking at income,” Armstrong said.

“That’s where the alternative lenders can come in and have a different risk appetite — to be able to say, we want to look at that cash flow of the business. Some of our clients have multiple properties — bank statement approach, investment properties, holdcos — stuff that’s just a little bit outside of what the traditional bank is.”

Joel Cote, chief operating officer at Haventree Bank, described the evolution as a reclassification rather than a demotion.

“It’s no longer, for many, a short-term solution,” he said.

“For many clients that fit this profile, the alt solution is the prime solution.”

As Canadian mortgage debt continues to swell past record levels, the proportion of borrowers whose income structures fall outside conventional bank parameters is only expected to grow.

Packaging files and building lender relationships

For Prakash Bector, vice president of sales and distribution at EQ Bank, the sharpest opportunity for brokers in the alt space lies in how they prepare and present files.

For self-employed clients in particular, income verification requires understanding the full shape of the business — revenue, overhead, how the client structures expenses — not just a line-15 figure.

“The more equipped you are upfront, the easier it’s going to be for all of us to be able to assess the deal and give you a quick answer and move the file along,” he said.

The panelists were united on one practical step that few brokers take: call the lender’s business development manager and ask directly how income is calculated.

Armstrong noted that of more than 100 brokers in the room, fewer than 2% had done so. That single conversation, he argued, can redefine a broker’s performance in the alt space.

Brokers looking to sharpen their edge with alternative lenders would do well to start there.

“Build the package for the lender,” he said. “If you build it for yourself, it doesn’t help the lender.”

Cote offered a clear summary of what separates approvals from declines.

“What kills deals are surprises,” he said. “The more info that we know upfront, the better equipped we are to try to navigate a solution.”

As artificial intelligence begins reshaping how mortgage brokers handle file complexity and client communication, the ability to build clean, transparent files quickly is only going to matter more.

items.title: Return-to-office trend poses new challenges for Canadian homebuyers
items.description: Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work
items.content: <p>Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639293254820279869.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lenders expect clarity on a borrower’s arrangement with their employer as companies ramp up expectations for in-office work
items.body:
A major pandemic-era trend was the movement of Canadians further away from their office location as remote-working arrangements became more and more prominent, helping facilitate migration into more affordable markets.

But a gradual ramping-up of return-to-office efforts by employers is raising questions about the future of that movement – and whether lenders will take a more rigorous approach to mortgage applicants who live far from their workplace.

Lenders are still generally receptive to borrowers living a long way from their workplace, but Durham Region-based mortgage broker Sherry Corbitt told Canadian Mortgage Professional that further clarification or assurance from employers about that arrangement remains commonplace.

“A lot of the times we’ll send in the job letter and the paystub, and then we’ll get back, ‘Please revise the job letter to say that there’s a hybrid, or what the obligation of in-office is,’” she said. “I would probably say I see that on half of my purchase files.”

A recent survey by real estate giant RE/MAX Canada showed a growing number of Canadians are prepared to make compromises to buy a property, including moving further away from their current location.

But Corbitt said lenders generally want answers as soon as a commute stretches beyond 100 kilometres. “They want to understand, ‘Does this client really plan to do a three-hour commute in the winter, or can they work from home?’ If it’s work from home, it’s checked and gone – the condition is waived,” she said.

“If it’s no, you have to commute for three hours, they start saying: ‘Well, are they paying rent somewhere? Are they living with family somewhere? Is there a shelter payment somewhere?’”

Shifting employer expectations change the borrower picture

Investors are reportedly flooding back into the office market in major urban centres like Toronto amid rising clamour from employers for their workers to spend at least a few days a week in the office.

The country’s top banks are stepping up efforts to bring back workers, while earlier this year the federal government’s Treasury Board said it was mandating a five-day office week.

The swing back toward employers’ in-office preferences, Corbitt said, is also impacting clients at renewal. “There’s a lot of back-to-work, which is biting a couple of people for sure,” she said. “I’ve had some clients call me and say, ‘I’ve been mandated back to work… I moved during COVID. How does that affect my renewal?’

“So then we discuss: Do you renew soon? Do we look at a different lender? Or do you get another job first? There’s a lot of strategies.”

First-time buyers gain ground in a sluggish market

While changing work arrangements are posing plenty of questions, one of the bright sides to a generally torrid 2026 housing market is that plenty of first-time buyers are finally finding opportunities to gain a foothold on the property ladder.

Prices have fallen across many markets amid milder competition and first-time buyers are now able to snag a property for between $500,000 and $600,000 that, Corbitt said, might have gone for $200,000 higher during the pandemic.

That price depreciation stands in stark contrast to the trend seen during the pandemic, when intense bidding wars often pushed offers well above list prices and saw many hopeful buyers overpowered in the market.

The ability to provide longer amortizations of up to 30 years is also providing extra breathing space, Corbitt added, even for buyers who could technically afford to pay on a 25-year schedule.

“We talk about the strategy of setting it at 30 years so you’re very comfortable with your payment,” she said, “and then once you’re in it, you can accelerate your payment by doing prepayments.”

But climbing interest rates are also presenting challenges for first-time buyers, while economic uncertainty has been exacerbated by the ongoing trade war with the US and rising inflation.

The cost-of-living crisis is still a real concern for many buyers, and Corbitt highlighted the reality that a high percentage of first-time entrants to the market don’t have a significant emergency fund to rely on after they’ve made their purchase.

“First-time buyers are using all their savings to get into a home,” she said. “There’s a lot of anxiety about not having any safety net to fall back on.”

Presenting a comprehensive slate of options to clients in those situations, Corbitt said, is the best way to keep them with a broker rather than defecting to a bank. “If you provide them security, then it’s not a conversation about rate,” she said.

items.title: What mortgage renewals are really costing Canadian borrowers
items.description: A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment
items.content: <p>A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639293222322937005.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new national survey surfaces the full price Canadians are paying beyond the monthly payment
items.body:
Rising mortgage renewal rates are hindering the financial goals of one in five Canadian Millennials and Gen X borrowers, according to new survey data that puts hard numbers to the cost pressures reshaping household finances.

The Great Delay 2026, commissioned by estate-planning platform Willful and conducted by Angus Reid Forum among 1,501 Canadian adults from September 1 to 10, found that 64% of respondents with housing payments saw those costs rise over the past year.

Nationally, 15% of Canadians identified rising mortgage renewal rates as a barrier to their financial goals, climbing to 25% among the “sandwich generation,” defined as those with at least one living parent and a child of any age.

Nearly half of that cohort, 48%, carry a mortgage, compared with 35% of Canadians overall.

“Canadians got more done with their money this year, and they still feel worse off,” said Erin Bury, CEO and co-founder of Willful.

The data arrives as brokers continue to navigate the tail end of Canada’s mortgage renewal wave, as holders of five-year terms originated at pandemic-era lows in 2020 and 2021 confront today’s substantially higher rates.

Mortgage payments squeeze household budgets

Nationally, 40% of Canadians say their position has worsened year over year, up from 37% in 2025, and 47% dipped into savings to cover everyday costs.

On average, respondents said they would need $818 more each month to reach their financial goals.

Notably, 22% of Canadians and 25% of the sandwich generation identified lower interest rates as the single change most likely to help them get there, making rate relief the second most commonly cited factor after a drop in everyday costs and inflation.

The survey’s generational mortgage data is particularly striking for brokers. Among all Canadian generations, Millennials and Gen X carry the highest mortgage rates – 45% and 47% respectively – yet represent the groups most squeezed by the renewal cycle.

Millennials face a particular bind: 45% hold a mortgage and 34% have a child under 18, making them among the most financially exposed households in the country. Only 17% have a will.

Homeownership aspirations are also being deferred, with 13% of Canadians delaying a home purchase in 2026, rising to 23% of Millennials.

The pressure is most acute within the sandwich generation. Nearly half, 48%, carry a mortgage compared with 35% of Canadians overall, and 25% cite rising mortgage renewal rates as a direct barrier to their goals, compared with 15% nationally.

With debt repayment costs up for 49% of that group against 44% of Canadians overall, 88% say they would need more monthly income to meet their goals.

Of those, 71% need at least $500 more per month, and 41% need $1,000 or more.

Lauren van den Berg, president and chief executive officer of Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) in Ottawa, drew a direct line from the data to the broker’s role.

“Renewal pressure is not just about interest rates,” she said in a Mortgage Professionals Canada survey on borrowers most exposed to payment shock.

“It is about how much room households have to absorb a higher payment. This research shows many borrowers are approaching renewal with thin payment buffers, which makes early advice, careful planning and access to the right mortgage options more important than ever.”

What brokers are hearing from renewal clients

Sarah Albert, a broker with Premiere Mortgage Centre in New Brunswick, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in August that the renewal cycle has generated a surge in refinancing as clients work to absorb higher costs.

“We have a ton of refinances right now,” Albert said.

“We’re basically resetting mortgages to 25, 30 years, consolidating some debt and actually saving them some money each month where they can kind of maintain their lifestyle.”

Albert stressed that the most effective tool for brokers navigating client renewal anxiety is direct, personal engagement – not digital workarounds.

“I have a lot of clients that are calling right now… We’re seeing a lot of panic,” she said.

“And then when they talk to us, they’re like, ‘Oh, I’m not a bad client.’ I keep saying to them, ‘You’re a better client than you think you are. You’re human. We just need to reset this and learn this lesson, and I’ve got you.’”

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s updated immigration levels plan is set to be unveiled in Thursday’s federal budget, multiple government sources tell CTV News.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney’s updated immigration levels plan is set to be unveiled in Thursday’s federal budget, multiple government sources tell CTV News.

The updated targets come as Canada’s population growth has seen a slowdown in the past two years. Carney, meanwhile, has sent recent mixed signals over the direction of immigration in Canada.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In September, the prime minister told the New York Times that Canada will eventually resume a “controlled increase” in its population once the immigration system remains fully under control, but he did not provide specifics.

Weeks later, Carney insisted his government will “not budge” from its goal of keeping national immigration levels sustainable.

Last year, the Carney government lowered and stabilized permanent resident admissions to 380,000 per year from 2026 to 2028. Targets for new temporary resident arrivals were also reduced to 385,000 in 2026 and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.

The moves were in response to significant increases in immigration in the early 2020s under former prime minister Justin Trudeau that led to pressures on housing and social services.

Data from Statistics Canada shows temporary residents experienced significant growth between 2021 and 2024, peaking at 7.6 per cent of Canada’s population in October 2024.

That prompted shifts under the late months of the Trudeau government, including caps on international students, and Carney’s 2025 federal election pledge to “return immigration to sustainable levels.”

‘Controlled increase’ in immigration

The recent lowered targets along with other measures, however, have contributed to Canada’s slow population growth. According to Statistics Canada, the country’s population reached an estimated 41,798,407 people on July 1, 2026, an increase of 189,425 people or 0.5 per cent from July 1, 2025 – marking the lowest July-to-July growth in total population size since 1944-45.

In October, the Bank of Canada concluded that Canada’s aging population and declining immigration is “reshaping” the economy by shrinking the workforce and shifting what people are consuming.

Another report from RBC in September, meanwhile, urged Canada to rethink its immigration strategy that “could get admissions back on track and avoid slipping into the kind of politically charged, counter-productive discourse taking hold in places like the U.S. and Europe.”

Some recommendations from RBC include stabilizing population growth to one per cent and balancing admissions.

“Without immigration, the country’s population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century,” RBC’s skills policy lead Jackie Pichette writes.

Asked in October about Carney’s recent comment alluding to a “controlled increase” in immigration, Immigration Minister Lena Diab pointed to the country’s slow population growth and the federal government’s “ambitious agenda.”

“We’ve taken a step backwards on immigration. Our population increase, it was the slowest population growth since World War II. Again, that’s not me saying it. That’s the numbers,” Diab said at the time. “We have an ambitious agenda. We are going to want to drive growth. We do need people.”

Conservatives expect ‘much lower’ levels

During that October announcement, Diab unveiled changes effective Nov. 3 to the express entry program that will award extra points for high-wage earners in a bid to drive economic growth and retain skilled newcomers.

The Conservatives, meanwhile, have been calling on the federal government to further reduce permanent residency admissions in the coming immigration levels plan.

“Let me be perfectly clear – the Conservative Party of Canada will vigorously oppose any efforts by Prime Minister Carney and his Liberal government to increase immigration,” Conservative MP and immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said in a statement in September in response to Carney’s New York Times interview.

“We will also continue to press for major decreases of immigration levels. We expect immigration levels to be set much, much lower in the upcoming immigration levels report.”

With files from CTV News’ Vassy Kapelos and Marieke Walsh

items.title: Laurentian Bank delists after 180 years as Fairstone deal closes
items.description: A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone
items.content: <p>A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639002802766554708.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A two-part transaction reshapes Canada’s banking landscape as B2B Bank moves to Fairstone
items.body:
Laurentian Bank of Canada has completed its two-part sale, ending 180 years as an independent publicly listed institution and placing control in the hands of two lenders with distinct strategic goals.

The transactions, first announced in December 2025, closed November 1.

Fairstone Bank of Canada acquired all of Laurentian’s common shares at $40.50 per share, a total of approximately $1.9 billion.

National Bank of Canada (NBC) simultaneously assumed roughly $8 billion in liabilities and acquired approximately $3.7 billion in assets from Laurentian’s retail and small and medium enterprise (SME) banking portfolios, according to the joint completion announcement.

Laurentian’s common shares are expected to be delisted from the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) at market close on November 3.

What changes for the broker channel

B2B Bank, Laurentian’s broker-facing subsidiary serving approximately 27,000 financial advisers and mortgage brokers across Canada, now operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Fairstone.

The transition extends Fairstone’s reach into broker-distributed lending, building on its standing as Canada’s largest alternative lender following the merger of Fairstone Bank and Home Trust Company completed in January 2025.

Carl De Souza, senior vice president and sector lead for North American financial institution ratings at Morningstar DBRS in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in December 2025 that Canada’s appetite for large-scale banking consolidation was nearly spent.

“There’s not much further merger and acquisition space in 2026 in the Canadian sense. I don’t know where it would come from. I think to most, the PC Financial acquisition was somewhat unexpected. So there could always be something like that. The Big Six might do some tuck-in acquisitions, but I wouldn’t say anything of a material nature,” De Souza said. 

Laurentian refocused as a commercial lender

Founded in 1846, Laurentian operated personal and commercial banking and capital markets businesses in Canada and the United States.

The restructured Laurentian will operate as a Fairstone subsidiary, concentrating on commercial real estate, inventory, and equipment financing with a particular emphasis on Québec.

“This important milestone marks the beginning of a new chapter for our organization and reinforces our position as a specialized commercial bank, allowing us to build on our strengths and focus on the areas where we can create the greatest value,” said Éric Provost, president and chief executive officer of Laurentian Bank of Canada.

Fairstone, a privately held lender with roots dating back to the 1920s, focuses on residential and commercial mortgages, consumer deposits, auto and retail financing and personal loans across more than 250 branches and digital channels. It is the parent company of mortgage market giant Home Trust.

Scott Wood, president and CEO of Fairstone Bank, said the rationale centred on diversification and scale.

“The acquisition of Laurentian Bank represents a significant step forward in the continued evolution of Fairstone Bank, enhancing the breadth and resilience of our business. Bringing together complementary businesses will diversify and scale our asset base and funding sources, support sustainable, profitable growth, and unlock opportunities to operate more effectively as we integrate our organizations,” Wood said.

For NBC, the transaction deepens its retail footprint in Québec.

“We are pleased to welcome new retail and SME clients shortly and provide them with access to National Bank’s full range of digital services, an expanded suite of financial products, our branch network and our business banking teams,” said Laurent Ferreira, president and CEO of National Bank.

National Bank was founded in 1859. It offers retail, commercial, wealth and capital markets services and reported $553 billion in assets as of July 31, 2025.

items.title: Expert: For Some, Homeownership Is Just A Dream
items.description:
For decades, buying a home was viewed as a rite of passage to adulthood. It represented stability, security, and the opportunity to build a future. Today, for many young people, it feels more like a fantasy than a realistic goal.

Recent polling and research have consistently shown that a growing number of young people no longer believe they will ever own a home. They don’t believe the housing crisis is being resolved.

While governments talk about affordability, youth do not see affordability improving in their daily lives.

Surveys of Ontarians aged 18 to 38 found that only 47% believe homeownership is achievable. More than one-quarter say it is not achievable at all, while another quarter are unsure. Young Ontarians are among the least optimistic people in Canada when it comes to their housing prospects.

A 2025 report commissioned by the Ontario Home Builders' Association found that young people in Ontario have "little hope" of buying a home. Eleven of 26 municipalities studied were deemed "completely unattainable" for middle-class households.

The report found that while house prices have more than doubled since 2005, inflation-adjusted wages have risen just 16%. In major markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, Guelph, and Barrie, homes now cost more than seven times annual pre-tax income.

Twenty-five years ago, the typical Ontario home cost roughly three to four times household income. Today, the ratio is closer to seven to nine times.

Not surprisingly, confidence has collapsed.

A housing outlook by the Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) paints a similarly grim picture. Only 12% of Ontarians believe housing will become more affordable over the next five years. More than one-quarter of aspiring homeowners now believe they will never buy a home.

Young people are often accused of being pessimistic. In this case, however, their skepticism is justified.

This is not to say there haven’t been some positive developments.

Governments have finally acknowledged the severity of the housing crisis. The federal and Ontario governments have introduced new temporary HST rebates and other measures aimed at improving affordability while some municipalities have begun exploring reductions in development charges (DCs).

Polling conducted by Abacus Data for OREA found that 75% of Ontarians support reducing municipal DCs and 72% support provincial limits on those charges. Most reject the notion that new homebuyers should bear the cost of growth-related infrastructure.

They are right.

DCs are a hidden tax on homeownership. While municipalities defend them under the principle that "growth should pay for growth," the practical effect is that first-time buyers and young families are forced to shoulder the cost of infrastructure that benefits entire communities. The charges are embedded in housing prices and financed through mortgages.

Reducing DCs won’t solve every housing problem. But it would directly reduce construction costs, improve project viability and lower the final purchase price of homes. It would also send a signal that governments are serious about tackling affordability rather than merely talking about it.

The consequences of failing to act extend far beyond the housing market.

Housing affordability is increasingly shaping life decisions. Young adults are delaying marriage, postponing family formation, and reconsidering where they live. Some are leaving Ontario altogether in search of more affordable opportunities.

Meanwhile, there is growing evidence linking housing costs to falling birth rates. Toronto's fertility rate has fallen to just 1.11 children per woman, lower than Canada's already weak national rate of 1.25, and far below the replacement rate of 2.1. Statistics Canada has found that 37% of Canadians aged 15 to 49 do not believe they can afford to have a child within the next three years.

When housing policy begins influencing whether people can buy homes, stay in a province or have children, the issue is no longer simply about real estate. It’s a question of economic sustainability.

Young Ontarians haven’t given up on homeownership. They still want the stability and security it provides. What they have given up on is the belief that current policies are producing meaningful change.

Until governments permanently reduce the tax burden on housing and DCs, and dramatically increase supply, their skepticism will remain justified. Youth are not losing faith in homeownership. Rather, they are losing faith that governments are prepared to do what it takes to make it attainable again.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.
