items.body:
With Alt- and B-lending no longer a niche solution, the best brokers are turning to the sector in increasing numbers – and in a recent panel at MortgageFest Canada, top lending executives in the sector gathered to discuss the processes brokers are using to improve approvals, reduce friction, and strengthen long-term lender relationships.

00:01 [music]
00:09 [music]
00:10 I'm pleased to introduce the next session, Winning the Alt Space: Placing, Packaging, and Positioning for Success.
00:17 Great. Welcome, guys. Enjoy.
00:19 Thank you all for coming, and I'm hoping we're going to have a nice collaborative panel. We're going to kick it off. We're going to start off nice and easy. This
00:27 one is going to be directed at Joe, but please feel free to all chime in. What are the most common alternative borrower
00:36 profiles? And when is alternative lending the right fit for a client?
00:41 I might be a little bit biased, but I'll say always. Um, the borrower profile in the altit, you know, kind of take a giant step back and think about what was
00:50 that profile back in the day? Bruised credit. We love to always say bad things happen to good people. At the same point in time, Bruce credit has evolved in
00:59 terms of the alt space is now anything alternative to prime big six credit
01:06 boxes. And what I love about the space is the growth, the depth and breadth of the relationships that we can have with our broker partners.
01:15 About in particular that customer profile, we've got customers everything from ranging to life circumstances
01:23 around say divorce, CRA, bankruptcies, small business owners. It's a real challenge in this market with tariffs
01:31 for small business owners to be able to make it through. However, I'll extend that to multiple properties, rental income, seasonal properties.
01:40 We see the entire gamut of what used to be prime borrowers are now alternative customer profiles.
01:48 And we actually, I would say, if anything, have started to redesign a lot of our workflows and partnership models with our brokers completely anchored around what the broker and client experience
01:55 looks like for this growing profile base.
02:03 It's like the box around the typical borrower is getting a little bit smaller, and now you're finding it's not just bruised credit. It's a lot more different client profiles. Do any of you have anything else to add on this?
02:11 Yeah, I guess I'll jump in. I mean, I agree 100% on that. I'll take it a little different. Like, the bruised credit's still always going to be there, but it's a
02:19 much smaller part than it was. I mean, 15, 20 years ago, it was double bankrupt and breathing, and you can get a mortgage. It's a little different now.
02:27 But I think when you look at it, it's the customers that have that unique income situation. It's customers that need somebody to look beyond just the line
02:35 15,000. I look at our profile. The average FICO score is 763.
02:40 That is actually, in some cases, it's outperformed some of the big six banks.
02:44 I think what you're looking at is what we're seeing on the alt side is it's entrepreneurs. It's clients with a great net worth that fall outside of
02:52 that bank box that you're talking about, but it's because of the qualification criteria. And that's the big thing that's happened over the last five or 10 years is with regulation, banks have
03:01 very, very specific ways of looking at income. And I think that's where the alternative lenders can come in and have a different risk appetite to be able to
03:09 say, you know what? We want to look at that cash flow of the business. Some of our clients have multiple properties, like, again, entrepreneurs, bank
03:17 statement approach, investment properties, holdcos, stuff that's just a little bit outside of what the traditional bank is.
03:25 The other part of the advantage is the market's gotten so big, so big banks, big six can focus on building their businesses off of that more traditional type of credit.
03:34 And there's more customers now that need that unique type of flexible verification or a different way of looking at the file.
03:40 Are there even any key signs anymore that a borrower is more suited to alternative versus prime? I know maybe a
03:48 while ago we would have said bruised credit, but is there one key differentiator that stands out?
03:57 I mean, look, I think it really depends on the client profile. Just to add a little bit, historically in the alt business, it was perceived as
04:04 a short-term solution for clients. In many cases now, the alt solution is the prime solution for these
04:11 clients. So, you've got clients that are perhaps self-employed or have part-time jobs or contract work or
04:19 multiple properties. There are lots of different opportunities, I think, where clients can fit that alt bucket.
04:28 I think one key point, though, is it's no longer for many a short-term solution. It is the best solution for many clients that fit that profile.
04:36 Yeah, I see for a lot of my business-for-self clients, it is a solution for them, more of a long-term solution. Now, for cash, what documentation, income and
04:45 down payment expectations should brokers understand to help improve underwriting efficiency?
04:51 Great question. So, I mean, income and down payment, right? Those are two easy things, right? Always run really smoothly, no problems at all. The
04:59 alt business is really no different than the prime business in terms of deals need to be qualified effectively and down payment needs to be sourced.
05:10 Some of the key differentiators, I'll start with income in particular. When you're looking at that self-employed or there's a shift, you're not really
05:18 focused so much on the individual earnings. That's part of it, but the real focus is what is the business actually generating?
05:26 So, you're doing a really cohesive deep dive on this client's business. What type of business do they run? Where do they get their
05:34 clients? What overhead expenses do they need to operate their business? It's a full overview of the actual business
05:42 rather than just focusing on their personal income. With that comes additional flexibility. The two main types of documentation you would use for
05:50 income would be either bank statements or business financials. Where the additional complexity comes for all of you is really understanding that
05:59 business profile for the customer. And the reality is, especially for small businesses, everyone operates it slightly differently.
06:07 We are seeing certain cases where sometimes personal expenses shift into business expenses. So, I'd say the key
06:15 point up front when you're looking at these deals and packaging them is just have a really good understanding of your client and their
06:24 income and the revenue and expenses that their business generates. The more equipped you are upfront, the easier
06:32 it's going to be for all of us to be able to assess the deal and give you a quick answer and move the file along.
06:38 Similarly with down payment, down payments coming from savings for 90 days and there's no movement in money. Great.
06:45 I don't think many of those scenarios exist anymore. So, very similar, like if down payment's coming from overseas, it's where's the paper trail? Like,
06:53 really understand where the money is coming from, be able to explain it and be able to back it up. But I'd say the big key differentiator is income and how you're assessing it.
07:02 For alt lenders, especially for those self-employed clients, it's really requiring a deep understanding of the client's business.
07:11 Did you have something to add? Yeah.
07:12 You know, I've been at all aspects of the business as a broker, a lender, an underwriter, and I truly believe a
07:19 well-packaged file is respect for not just you, the lender, but also the client as well. It's important to make sure you
07:26 deliver the package properly. It's all about your customer at the end of the day.
07:30 Yeah. And time savings, right? Not only for us, for the clients, realtors, underwriters, just to keep the file moving along smoothly.
07:39 And certainly having an understanding of the full file before we send it in. Where do you see brokers most often missing the mark on
07:47 this? Is this what it is? The package? Is it the business financials?
07:52 What's the biggest slip? I don't think they're missing the mark per se, but I think the challenge is, and maybe I'll ask everyone here, how many
08:01 people in this room have called a lender and asked them to tell them how to calculate income?
08:09 Okay, I want to, like, there's over 100 brokers in this room who every day send deals in, and 99% of you have not asked the people who are making a decision.
08:17 And that's the difference. How each one of us looks at income is going to be different. That's why the four of us can grow. We all look at it a little differently.
08:26 Part of the biggest changes as well is to be productive and improve processing. We're all creating new processes. We're all using checklists and
08:33 forms, AI-built tools so that we can streamline the process. A lot of times what I find with brokers is, here's my
08:42 package, and you need to figure out the income into it. That's going to take us three, five, seven days. And if you really
08:49 want a lender investigating and looking and finding things, they'll find stuff and they'll have more questions. If
08:57 you actually take the time and ask them how it is. So, I'll share a personal story. Many years ago, when I used
09:04 to do deals, my old underwriter, I will point her out because she hates it, is in the room. I took her out for a coffee and I asked her how to do deals. And I
09:14 turned into that company's single largest referral source for seven-plus years. And the files were simple. I think they were. She'll tell you another
09:22 story, I'm sure. But that's the trick. I encourage every one of you: call a BDM, ask to meet with an underwriter, and
09:30 ask the simplest question: How do you calculate income? And they will tell you every tip, trick, and factual thing. And then build the package for the lender.
09:41 Because if you build it for yourself, it doesn't help the lender. And I think if you want a smooth, simple process, that's the benefit. And there are
09:50 advantages or disadvantages to that. You can negotiate, you can have some exceptions, but the reality is you're
09:58 asking a lender to approve a file. They need to prove it to their policy. So that's my suggestion. Thank you to the two people who put their hands up,
10:06 but to the other hundred of you, I encourage you to do that.
10:10 Yeah, I love that. And I'm going to just both agree with you and build on that. We have an entire sales team of BDMs.
10:18 Their job is to work with you, for you.
10:22 Plain and simple. They don't run operational processes. They don't do internal documentation. They are there as reference guides for you. So, if we
10:30 only got two people putting their hands up, I would highly recommend that for every single one of these lenders: pick up the phone, call your BDM, and say,
10:39 "I've got a deal." And honestly, my biggest piece of advice: What's the story? The BDM will help you figure out
10:47 how to package that, what you need to ask the client that maybe you didn't even think of asking yet, but that is their reference source for you. Pick up
10:56 the phone, call them. They're going to have all the answers for you. And if they don't, I promise you they can get it to you within minutes.
11:01 Yeah. Every BDM that we call, they're very helpful. They want to see you get that deal across the finish line. And we're not in the A space. It's
11:09 not two T4s and a pay stub. And you all treat income, especially with a bank statement, differently. So, really packaging the file properly, direct
11:17 communication, as well as telling the story and having that open line. Right? Is that a good summary?
11:24 Well, it's not just a beacon score anymore. No, it's not just a beacon score. Yeah.
11:27 Yeah, I mean, we could do the beacon scores, but it's not just the beacon score, right? Okay, this one's for Cam.
11:33 How can brokers position alt solutions as part of a broader sustainable client strategy rather than the last resort?
11:41 Honestly, it's about strategy for brokers. When they look at a file, it shouldn't be about, "Can I get an approval?" It should be about building these clients, looking for one to three
11:50 years down the road versus, "Hey, can I at least get an approval for this deal?"
11:55 It's about building the deal out, helping your client, finding an exit strategy at the end of the day, moving them to the next phase, to the next
12:02 lender or wherever it may be. At MCAN, I'm trying to get a little prop here. We do have a graduation program that will help clients move to the next phase of the transition of the deal.
12:13 Yeah. And it's looking at the whole file and their real life, right? What problem are we trying to solve? Is there even a problem that we're trying
12:21 to solve? Do they just not fit the A profile? It's all about the journey.
12:25 Yeah. Does anybody else have anything to add on this?
12:28 Yeah, I'd agree. I think it comes down to, again, understanding the client situation, and I'll go back to what I said earlier. I think for many clients
12:35 that fit this bucket, the alt solution is their prime solution. Like, it's the best option for them. Rate
12:43 is important, no doubt about it. But when you factor in, let's say you're looking at the two options of the best rate in the market versus the most
12:52 suitable solution, what would the client need to do to their business or from an income standpoint to qualify for that
12:59 best rate? And then run an analysis: Is it feasible? Can they do it? How much time would it take them? How much would
13:06 it cost them to actually shift how they structure their business to be able to qualify for that lowest rate? So, I think another part is just shifting away
13:14 from the actual rate conversation and finding the solution that fits best for the client's profile. And many of
13:22 the clients that we finance every day, and Grant mentioned the FICO score, but we're very similar. These are very strong client profiles, but these are
13:30 the best solutions for their current income or equity situation.
13:36 Yeah. Because for some clients, we're placing them. It's not, again, just a stopgap. This
13:44 is more of a longer-term solution for them. How can we help? How can us brokers help clients understand that and pave that path for them?
13:52 So, I mean, one anecdote I've got: during COVID, rates were obviously very low in 2021. We remember those
13:59 good old days. At one point, our five-year fixed term was at 2.59. Do you know how many clients took us up on the five-year fixed term? Any guesses? Close to zero.
14:12 The vast majority of those clients ended up renewing or moving to another alternative lender. Just a proof point and an example where this really
14:20 is, for most clients, the long-term solution. So, just thinking around the most suitable term for their situation
14:27 is also an important piece of the puzzle.
14:29 Yeah. And in some cases, the spread between a conventional and the alternative side, it's not that great, right? It's not that big of a
14:37 spread. Explaining to the clients why this is a good, long-term solution for them. Again, say if we're talking about business-for-self, self-employed. Anybody else have anything to add?
14:46 Like I said earlier, it's not always about beacon score. It's not always about rate. It's finding the right lender to fit your client, the right
14:53 exit strategy for your client, preparing your client for that next phase. For sure, you have to be ready for that journey all the way.
15:00 Maybe add one thing. Alternative space as the lender of last resort? I'd say as
15:07 far as the thought process around that, no longer applies. There are millions of Canadians that do not fit the prime big six credit box on a full-time basis.
15:19 We're going to do a little Q&A with the crowd. This is not scripted. No, not at all. I love Q&A.
15:25 I like to go off script. My team hates me for it, which is a lot of fun. Of all the brokers in the room, can you please put your hand up and keep it up for a sec?
15:35 All right, keep up.
15:38 If you have never submitted an alt deal, put your hand down.
15:44 All right. So, you know what we're talking about. If you think about it, you can put your hands down now, or you can keep up. I mean, that could be fun.
15:53 The alternative space, you already know that there's a need for, and if you're having conversations with your customers, and for any of you who did, because I did
16:01 see a couple of hands go down, by the way, everybody else is clearly eating lunch. For every single one of them, you've got to build your business around the
16:10 client and that client need. Cash was talking about BFS. There's a lot of different needs, there's a lot of different programs and criteria and
16:19 qualification programs that are out there. Your ability to understand those. Again, go back to the BDM conversation.
16:26 You don't need to know every single lender's exact criteria. We're there to help you figure that out. We're there to
16:33 help you. And as I tell my team all the time, brokers are small business owners.
16:38 This is your business. We are there to support you in that. And in particular, this isn't about us building a lending
16:47 portfolio. This is actually all about building a partnership with you. And building that partnership with you is actually about creating a great
16:54 experience for you, a great experience for the client so that your small business thrives, so that your reputation and referrals will come
17:03 through on the back of what you hopefully get as a great experience from all four of us. Look for those opportunities when you're looking at clients to not just say it's not just
17:12 about rate, it's the terms and conditions that come along with every single one of those programs or products at the different lenders. And if you
17:19 need to know, we've got Sandy and Nelly from the team right here, that are more than happy to pick up the phone and help you figure that out.
17:27 I'm gonna add in on that. I think there's also a big change with some of the alt lenders. Many years ago, oh, there's just an alt lender, they just do mortgages, and you know, a year
17:35 later, we'll switch you to the bank with the branches, the bank accounts, and sorry again, but three of the four lenders up here are actually full-service banks. Like, that's a big
17:43 change. And I think when you're now talking to your customers, you used to say, "Oh, it's okay. Go to this lender.
17:48 All they do is mortgages or an alt lender. You go there for a year. We'll switch you to a real bank later." Three of us have actually some of
17:56 Canada's best high-interest-rate savings accounts. I got to commend you on the World Cup, like the soccer card, the yellow card was quite good. I'll give
18:03 you that credit. But that's the difference today. When you actually refer your customers to some of the alternative lenders now, you're actually referring them to a full banking package for them. They can get a bank account.
18:13 They can get a savings account. They can get their GICs there. There's lots of other services. So, I actually suggest to you to look beyond just the mortgage.
18:21 When you're actually positioning a client, you're talking about rate. You actually can refer them to a bank in some cases and help them position that solution going forward.
18:29 It's wonderful. Well, this question is for you. From a lender, and I think I know the answer. It's kind of a two-parter. From a lender's perspective,
18:37 what makes a file easy to approve? I'm sure it's going to be part of what we've already covered. And the second part is what separates a broker from a lender's preferred partners?
18:48 So, I think we talked a little bit about it before. The brokers that we love to work with are the ones that actually have taken the time to know our products. The ones that have sat down with the BDMs have called in.
18:57 They're fully transparent. They will say, "Hey, look, I've got this dog's breakfast of a deal, or the income I'm not sure, or I need some help." And they actually collaborate.
19:06 Just throw in a file everywhere. There's a gentleman in the room. I don't want to out him, but a number of months ago, we put together a very
19:13 complex file. Social media income, large net worth client, like gig economy. It
19:20 was not an easy file to put together. He made the call. He's like, "How do we put this file together?" And we found a way
19:27 to take a very complex file that I probably, if I told you the story, would sound like not a deal that we normally would put together. But we were able to look
19:35 beyond the documentation and actually collect the documents. And the one thing I'll say about this broker was every time we asked for something, he went and
19:43 got it. And it wasn't like, "You don't need this." And I don't know how many of you have said to a lender, "Oh, you don't need this." What's our money? Like, and we may actually.
19:53 We can do that.
19:54 We could also say we're not approving it. Like, I think there's that partnership. So, the best brokers are the
20:03 ones that we look at and say, "How do we work together on a file? How do we find a solution and actually collaborate and not become adversaries?"
20:10 Yeah. The ones that take the time to know your products, that take the time to communicate and package a file properly, obviously, right?
20:17 I just add, I mean, tough files or situations, those are all things we can work with. We're all a scrappy bunch. We've got amazing teams
20:26 that can roll up our sleeves and try to figure solutions out. What kills deals are surprises. The more info that
20:35 we know upfront, the better equipped we are to try to navigate a solution. A little plug for us:
20:42 you can call Equitable First. If we can't help, we'll pass it off.
20:46 Oh, who's second there? Come on. Putting you on the stage. I'm just—But no, that's really it. Again, it's just going back to really understanding your deal and don't shy
20:54 away from the issues. Be forthright about it. Let us know where the challenges are. We'll all hit it head-on and try to figure out a solution.
21:04 Anything else that brokers can do to build trust? That's actually my first line on it.
21:09 Trust and consistency. Having been an underwriter before, nothing worse than not understanding what the deal is about and the deal's been submitted. Like,
21:17 tell us the story. Tell us about your deal. Tell us about the property.
21:20 Explain the whole process because alt deals aren't hard to approve.
21:24 All deals can be challenging to approve if we don't have all the information in front of us. So, if you work with us in building a deal out, everybody here can
21:32 approve that deal. Every deal has a story behind it. Every deal can make sense. Find the right lender for your deal.
21:39 And I'll add on to that. I think Frack said it as well. When you get up against something, so if the down payment comes in and it is a wire transfer from somewhere else,
21:47 don't try and provide another document around it. Deal with it head-on. "Hey, look, this came in." Hello, I got the NOA and it shows some taxes outstanding.
21:56 Okay, what's going on? Well, they're going to pay them today. This is what's happening, or the wire transfer came from here. There are ways to deal with it, but this is where, if the lender
22:04 discovers it and the lender asks, it's very different to change the narrative once the cat's out of the bag. Come to us and be honest and say, "Look, I
22:13 have a problem." Yeah. The red flag is made.
22:15 Yeah. It's better for you to put the red flag up of a problem and then come and ask for a solution than us to
22:24 put the red flag up and assume the worst.
22:26 Oh, yeah. You don't want something pulled and called in the 11th hour as a broker.

22:35 Answer your phone when the underwriter calls you. I'm sure you could all echo that.
22:39 No lender actually wants to pull a file. That is the worst call to say.
22:44 It's like, "Hey, we've worked together for three months. Your client's got a house closing on Thursday. I'm sorry."
22:49 Nobody wants to do that. We want to fund the deal. We want to make it happen, and we have to just figure out how to get through it.
22:56 And honestly, a good broker looks at their income documents before sending them to the lender versus just forwarding them through. Like,
23:02 understanding that some brokers I even work with actually do the verbals themselves before sending them to the lender, so they know what they're looking for, what they're actually going
23:11 to get the responses from when they call the employer.
23:13 Oh, yeah. You can't just send a file in without doing that. Absolutely not.

23:20 Where do you, and this is kind of a question for all of you. You can kind of jump in. Where do you see the biggest opportunity for brokers to become more

23:47 to two or three per on the alt side, or just alt-side lending private. Just narrow it down, get to know your lenders, understand their products, and
23:56 this way it works better for you. I'm going to add on that. I think the biggest opportunity is embracing change with AI. And I'm not worried about AI

24:44 years, or five years, sorry, and that tested a lot of things. You're now going to see 25 years of technology innovation happen

items.description:

The post Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian banks see more losses from delinquent mortgages in their future—a lot more losses. Mortgage loss expectations have 3x since 2019.
items.body:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses has more than doubled over the past four years.

Canadian Banks Expect Mortgage Losses To Climb Sharply

Ratio of expected credit losses to total residential mortgage balances.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Lenders need to be prepared for losses on bad loans. It doesn’t matter how much borrowers are vetted; the reality is some won’t be fully repaid. To account for this, lenders record an allowance for credit losses—an estimate of the money they do not expect to recover. It reflects expected losses, not just losses that have already occurred. Those expectations have risen sharply.

The CMHC compared each bank’s mortgage portfolio against its allowance for credit losses. The median—half of banks are better, half are worse—had an allowance equivalent to $149 per $100,000 in mortgages in Q2 2026, up 13.2% from a year earlier. That share has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, more than doubling. It has roughly tripled (+202.8%) since Q2 2019, back in the before times.

Keep in mind that these measure expected losses relative to mortgage balances. The banks are preparing for higher losses on each dollar lent, and they’ve lent a lot more dollars over that period. Their expectations of losses have grown alongside their mortgage portfolio over the past 7 years.

Canadian Mortgage Losses Expected To Rise Further At Some Banks

The median bank’s increase is sharp, but it hides a much sharper climb at some banks. The 75th percentile, the threshold for the top 25% of banks, saw allowances reach $337 per $100,000 in mortgages, up 47.9% from last year. The share is more than double (+126%) the median, and the highest in the data going back to 2015.

Canadian Mortgage Loss Expectations Grew At 3 In 4 Banks

Most banks expect higher mortgage losses, with roughly 3 in 4 reporting higher allowances than a year earlier. That share was just 53% a year prior, an already tenfold increase from the 5% recorded in Q2 2022. The share of banks reporting higher expected losses has gone from only 1 in 20 banks to 3 in 4 over just four years.

While the amount remains small relative to total mortgage debt, the increase is hard to ignore. Banks are preparing to lose more of each dollar lent, and more lenders expect losses to grow. That also only captures part of the rising pressure, with distress rising even faster among mortgage investment entities (MIEs).

items.title: As hopes of a Canada-US deal rise, here’s what’s at stake for housing
items.description: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.content: <p>Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639292419264737498.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Positive remarks by Prime Minister Carney and President Trump have fuelled talk of a deal, potentially brightening the mortgage outlook
items.body:
Formal talks between Canada and the US on a resolution to the tariff war could begin soon after prime minister Mark Carney’s Sunday social media post describing a productive recent discussion on the issue with US president Donald Trump.

Trade tensions have weighed against Canada’s economic outlook since the beginning of last year and emerged as a significant factor in the housing market’s continued malaise, pushing plenty of potential homebuyers to the sidelines and damaging consumer confidence.

While discussions between US and Canadian negotiators have yet to resume, a positive resolution to the trade war could have big implications for the national housing market.

Prospects for a 2027 recovery, some mortgage professionals say, could hinge massively on whether tariff tensions ease.

And Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) has highlighted how the trade war is worsening the mortgage strain for many borrowers in tariff-impacted parts of the country such as Southern Ontario, which has borne the brunt of US levies on steel, aluminum, automotive vehicles and parts, and agricultural products.

With homebuilding also taking a hit, the national housing agency’s deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional a swift end to the trade war could potentially improve the currently dire construction outlook.

“I’m a little bit concerned on the housing supply situation that higher interest rates are affecting developers,” he said. “Now on that side, if the situation were resolved, then maybe developers would have a lot more confidence in home construction.

“From a long-term affordability [perspective], that would be positive. I think if the overall uncertainty lowered… it would give renewed confidence to people who want to go out and buy a home. If you knew the dispute was over, I think that greater certainty would help the overall economy.”

Leaders’ comments suggest potential relief for borrowers ahead

Last week, Trump told a rally in Michigan that the trade war could be settled “pretty soon,” as he stepped up campaigning ahead of the crucial midterm elections, set to take place on November 3.

Trump and Carney’s recent statements mark the first hint of a possible détente since an end to tariff negotiations in August triggered a sudden escalation in the trade war.   

Ab Iorwerth said the ongoing trade war is part of the reason mortgage strain seems worse in Southern Ontario than other parts of the country, even though there’s no sign of a wider mortgage meltdown caused by rising arrears.

“There’s a lot of protection within the system so I don’t think we’re looking at a systemic issue, but there’s a lot of people being adversely impacted by what’s happening to them individually,” he said. “And I think a lot of households are facing challenges with these higher interest rates that they’re bearing and the uncertainty over the trajectory of mortgage rates.

“There’s still that lingering concern over inflation and then there’s uncertainty on the macroeconomic front with trade. So I think all of this is creating a lot of stress for individual households about what might happen.”

Iran and inflation add further complications for housing

While tariffs were the defining story of 2025 for the Canadian economy, they’ve been joined this year by surging fuel prices because of the war in Iran – another curveball that could complicate the picture even if the trade war ends.

Those higher fuel prices have sparked fears of a wider spillover into headline inflation, one of the main reasons the Bank of Canada opted to hike its benchmark interest rate last week for the first time in over three years.

Against that backdrop, the central bank doesn’t see the housing market bouncing back in 2027 – although it underlined the positive effects an end to the trade war could potentially have.

A Canada-US deal reducing tariffs “would increase exports and business investment, boosting employment and incomes,” the BoC said in its latest Monetary Policy Report. “Higher demand could increase the pass-through from higher energy prices. The removal of counter-tariffs would provide an offset.”

items.content: <p>Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0270_639292444699523088.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Haventree’s COO talks lending trends and the ever-evolving Canadian borrower
items.body:
The alternative lending space is changing – and as the big banks continue tightening their lending criteria, alt lenders are seeing their market share grow. At MortgageFest, we caught up with Haventree Bank chief operating officer Joe Cote to hear his thoughts on current trends and what’s in store for the sector down the line.

[00:00] There's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s, but we're talking about life happens. Brokers are small business owners. This affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years and the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers.

[00:30] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So, next up we have Joe Cote, Chief Operating Officer at HipBilt Bank, whose booth we see just over here. Have you been having many productive conversations with brokers today?

[00:40] Joe Cote: Lots of discussions. I certainly think that there's been a lot of changes throughout the industry, specifically with HipBilt, which is very exciting. And having a lot of brokers come back and are interested to see, you know, tell me more. Tell me what you're doing. We're hearing a lot of exciting things that have been happening over the course of the last 6 to 12 months. Tell me what's happening over the course of the next 6 to 12 months and how can we partner together?

[01:00] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And the event is happening at a really interesting time for the industry. I mean, not that we haven't had any non-eventful times over the past few years. It's just been one thing after the next. But 2026, how are you assessing the market this year? How's it been?

[01:13] Joe Cote: I think obviously the market has had a fairly large impact on a lot of brokers and a lot of lenders, the community at large. We are still very happy and fortunate with our position and our performance so far this year. We've got great partners. I think that value proposition that we have certainly been working on has been what, the proof in the pudding of being able to look to those partners. We've got a lot of partners that have come back. I think that they're very excited with the service, the products, and the relationships that we've built. And from an overall performance standpoint, we're going to finish the year actually fairly strong and we got some good growth prospects for 2027.

[01:45] Fergal McAlinden: I was interested to hear, Joe, from lenders about borrower types. We know that they've evolved a lot over the past few years. I'm wondering if there's a specific type of borrower that you feel best placed to cater to in the current market.

[01:57] Joe Cote: I think the short answer to that is there's not a very simple straightforward borrower type anymore. Well, I think one of the opportunities has certainly been around the evolution of the alt space and how it's very much part of the prime offering now. And it used to be around bruised credit, which is still very much the case and will always be part of the ideal client profile that the alt space was built off of.

[02:18] But now we look at the tightening credit box from a lot of the larger Schedule 1 banks. That business flow, as it's been tightening, has actually been coming into the alternative space. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. We're talking about great credit scores that are well into the 700s, low 800s. But we're talking about life happens. We're talking about divorces. We're talking about CRA. Multiple properties, business for self.

[02:43] It doesn't necessarily mean bruised credit anymore. It just means maybe not as simple from a credit profile standpoint. So, we are truly running the entire gamut of what I would say is the alternative space is now alt A through to what was bruised credit before. And I'd love to see the evolution of the space and the value that we're bringing back to the Canadian consumers.

[03:04] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. And I think that evolution, nobody's expecting that to slow anytime soon, especially with how the market is this year and some of the challenges being faced by buyers. When it comes to brokers, how have you been dealing with them this year? Are there any kind of approaches you've been keeping in mind with brokers?

[03:19] Joe Cote: Yeah, a big emphasis of our partnership model with brokers has been, how do we just focus on building our processes, our expectations, our interaction models completely around the broker community. And thinking about brokers as small business owners.

[03:34] I've been saying this a lot just recently on stage. I think the biggest thing was around brokers are small business owners. It is all about the experience. It's about the referral business. And if they land a great client experience based on the partnership that they have with the lender, that client's going to come back. They're going to refer more business.

[03:52] And that alternative space, again, especially in the small business community and or gig economy, we've got so many borrowers that are looking for solutions that they didn't even know existed before. So, we've basically repositioned, I would say, a lot of our processes and policies to be built around brokers and the client experience, keeping that really at heart.

[04:10] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Looking ahead, 2027, hard as it is to believe, is just around the corner. Any trends that you're keeping an eye on or anything that you're expecting to be a big factor next year?

[04:20] Joe Cote: It's too fast. I miss summer already. I would say the trend, if anything, is probably going to be continuing. If you think about it, a couple of things. One has been the compounding effect of the interest rate environment, the tariffs, both in terms of just cost of goods as well as taxation on it, especially for small business owners.

[04:40] All those financing needs actually aren't going away. The financing needs are going to increase, especially if you think about this affordability issue has now compounded for 5 years. That's taxing a lot of Canadians, and that problem's not going to get any easier in the current environment.

[04:56] Not only what's happening with Canada and the US, but certainly I think in terms of the interest rate environment over the course of the next 12 months, there's not a single person that's expecting interest rates to stay flat. In that increasing environment, it's going to only compound the problem, and brokers are going to need to understand that business model.

[05:15] They're going to need to find ways to actually support their clients who are going to have needs, and knowing full well that the traditional means of prime sourcing is not necessarily going to be as viable as it used to be historically. And the alternative space is going to be, I think, a huge eye-opener for a lot of the brokers that are not currently accessing the alt space like they should be.

[05:27] Fergal McAlinden: For sure, and on that rate question, as you mentioned, I think we're all just strapped in waiting to see what happens on the bond market and on trade war and everything.

[05:34] Joe Cote: Yeah.

[05:34] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah, the only thing that's certain is that we have more uncertainty ahead, I think, is the way to put it. Maybe just one last word on the event, Joe. Have you met your target audience, and we'll be seeing you next year?

[05:43] Joe Cote: Absolutely. It's been wonderful, actually. Not only have I met, from an audience perspective, everybody in terms of our partners, as well as potential net new partners, both in terms of brokers, as well as a lot of other broker ancillary partners here.

[05:58] I think about the technology providers, I think about net new products that are coming on the market. I can point to a couple over there, which I just think are phenomenal in terms of the innovation that is showcased at the event, and I love being part of it, hearing the stories, how we can better service our clients.

[06:12] And looking at these partner solutions on how we can kind of improve the experience, I will definitely be back.

[06:15] Fergal McAlinden: Love to hear it. Okay, great stuff. Thank you for stopping by. Much appreciated. Then enjoy the rest of the event.

[06:19] Joe Cote: Thanks for having me.

items.title: Ontario credit unions lift profits as 90-day loan arrears climb
items.description: Early mortgage delinquency eased in Q2, but regulator data shows deeper arrears quietly building
items.content: <p>Early mortgage delinquency eased in Q2, but regulator data shows deeper arrears quietly building</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639292407563693929.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Early mortgage delinquency eased in Q2, but regulator data shows deeper arrears quietly building
items.body:
Ontario credit unions grew assets and posted sharply stronger year-over-year profits in the second quarter of 2026, even as deeper loan arrears kept building, according to the latest Sector Outlook Report from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA).

Sector assets across the 48 institutions reached $106.47 billion at June 30, up 4.24% year over year.

Return on average assets (ROAA), the regulator’s core profitability measure, rose to 46 basis points from 30, as deposit costs fell faster than loan income.

One basis point equals 0.01%.

Credit union mortgage delinquency eases, but deeper arrears build

Residential mortgages remain the sector’s anchor. Credit unions held $57.92 billion in home loans at quarter-end, up 2.68% year over year, while commercial lending rose 1.97% to $27.44 billion.

The share of residential mortgages more than 30 days past due slipped to 1.13% from 1.15% in the first quarter, helping total 30-day delinquency record its first quarterly decline since the third quarter of 2024.

Year over year, though, mortgage delinquency was up 21 basis points, and commercial delinquency jumped 98 basis points to 2.80%.

The report’s tables point to strain further down the pipeline.

Loans more than 90 days delinquent rose to 1.08% of the total book from 0.99% in the first quarter and 0.71% a year earlier, while loan-loss allowances jumped 37.2% to $399 million.

Five of the 48 credit unions posted negative returns.

That mirrors the wider province, where Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) expects Ontario mortgage arrears to keep worsening until mid-2027.

CMHC deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth flagged the regional split in an October interview on trade-driven rate volatility and arrears.

“We’re watching arrears and delinquencies very closely. They’re particularly acute in Toronto, less so in Vancouver,” ab Iorwerth said.

“It’s just that they’re going up quite rapidly and it’s a source of concern. Maybe I should extend it beyond Toronto to include southern Ontario as well – but then you have places like Alberta where the economy remains strong and arrears and delinquencies remain contained.”

Jessica Rickerby, President of CMBA-ON, and Aled ab Iorwerth, Deputy Chief Economist at CMHC, warn that rising interest rates could further challenge housing affordability and prolong mortgage renewal pressures for Canadian borrowers. https://t.co/9P0c7D7qBi — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 2, 2026

What does the FSRA outlook mean for broker files?

The quarter predates tighter policy: the Bank of Canada held at 2.25% through June, then raised its rate to 2.50% on October 28.

Credit unions enter that shift with liquidity up 45 basis points to 12.88% and borrowings down 25.25%.

Lenders in the broker channel are already sharpening scrutiny. Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, spoke on a MortgageFest Canada panel on prime lending in September.

“We are very focused on making sure that the story and the documentation and the numbers align,” she said.

“Having those conversations upfront and telling that clear and concise story is going to allow underwriters to make a decision faster.”

FSRA said it issued the first edition of its Enhanced Data Collection Supplemental Report in September, with the next edition expected in the first quarter of 2027.

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories include Canada’s real estate spreading beyond Ontario and BC, and the CMHC warns mortgage arrears are set to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian GDP Stalls, Propped Up By Retail And Credit Cards

Canadian economic output is starting to struggle. Real GDP was flat for a second straight month in August, with only 9 out of 20 industrial sectors showing growth. Stalling appears to be an optimistic take though, as the details are a little more ominous. The pillars supporting the data were higher retail sales (mostly food) and credit card use. In other words, grocery spending and credit card debt are keeping the economy afloat. That’s more concerning given the increasing use of credit cards to make ends meet, according to TransUnion.

Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse

The arrears rate at Canadian banks has made an aggressive climb and it’s not over, warns the CMHC. The CBA arrears rate has more than doubled from record lows over the past 5 years, hitting 0.29% in July—an 11-year high. The rate will climb through mid-2027, the end of the agency’s forecast period. They cite price corrections in BC and Ontario persisting as the key reason. However, prices are near record highs in other provinces and have only just begun to correct, suggesting risk is further to the upside.

Bank of Canada Sees Elevated Inflation Into 2028, Housing To Remain Weak

The Bank of Canada’s (BoC) got 99 problems and inflation’s just one—until 2028, at least that’s what they think. This week the BoC hiked its overnight rate to 2.5%, its first hike in over 3 years. Higher energy prices will trickle into broader consumer inflation, warns the BoC. As a result, headline CPI’s annual growth will remain above 3% into late 2027, returning to the 2% target by mid-2028. Just 2 more years to flatten the (inflation) curve?

Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces

Prices across the country surged when rates were cut in 2020. The national index has fallen 22.5% since prices peaked in 2022, when rates began to normalize. However, that correction was almost entirely the work of Ontario and—to a lesser extent—BC. The rest of the provinces remain near record highs, but that may be finally changing. Prices in some of those provinces have recently begun to make record-setting declines.

Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply

BoC researchers looked at the impact of monetary stimulus on housing supply. They found that rate cuts during a housing boom boost home building by 6%, but only 20% of that is due to financing. The remaining 80% of stimulus comes from the excess demand, as profits and prices rise too. They warn ignoring shelter costs during a housing boom can lead to an aggressive climb in prices. However, there’s an area of shelter inflation the BoC should ignore—mortgage interest. Mortgage interest’s inclusion in CPI creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Cutting rates reduces mortgage interest, signaling the need for more rate cuts. It’s a problem we’ve noted before, warning the circular logic is avoided by most countries.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC

Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate at banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, 52% higher than last year and 5x the low in 2022. That’s only the bank rate though, which makes the picture look better than reality. High-risk borrowers get booted to mortgage investment entities (MIEs), where risk is exploding. MIEs have seen the arrears rate around Greater Toronto surge from 3% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026, 3x the national MIE rate. They may only be a small share of national activity, but the bulk of their business is concentrated in one area—along with risk.

items.body:
The Canadian economy has stalled, and the details offer little reassurance. Real GDP was flat in August for a second straight month, according to Statistics Canada (StatCan). Retail and credit card activity helped support output, an ominous combination as credit industry reports point to rising balances and delinquencies. The agency’s preliminary September estimate suggests that stagnation would be good news compared to what lies ahead.

Canada’s Economy Stalls For A Second Consecutive Month

Canadian economic output stalled for another month. Following a flat July, real GDP remained “essentially unchanged” in August. Just 9 of 20 industrial sectors expanded, with goods-producing industries rising 0.1% but tamed by a 0.1% drop in services. The stagnation follows massive jumps in April (+0.6%), May (+0.3%), and June (+0.4%), highlighting an abrupt and rapid loss of momentum.

Retail and Credit Card Activity Helping To Prop Up the Economy

The latest GDP report shows the economy may be living on borrowed time. One of the key areas of growth is retail output, rising 1.2% in August, led by vehicle dealers and food retailers. Also providing a boost was finance and insurance, which advanced 0.2%, with banking climbing 0.3% despite a slow mortgage market. The agency notes the growth in the latter was driven by non-mortgage lending activity, specifically credit cards.

That specific data point sounds more concerning when paired with TransUnion comments. The consumer credit reporting agency recently warned of rising balances and delinquency rates for consumers. They noted that consumers are increasingly relying on credit cards to smooth consumption. To be blunt, the read here isn’t very optimistic—consumer spending is helping to prop up the economy while borrowers increasingly rely on credit cards to make ends meet.

Canadian GDP Expected To Contract In September

Unfortunately, things are set to get worse according to the agency’s advance estimates. StatCan’s preliminary numbers point to a 0.1% drop in real GDP in September. Manufacturing and mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction are expected to lead the decline. However, the agency estimates average economic output in Q3 will still be 0.3% higher than in Q2, despite the loss of monthly momentum.

The figures also largely pre-date the latest tariff escalation. The U.S. imposed escalation only took effect in the final days of August, making September the first full month under those measures. It intensifies further as the first full month of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs won’t be seen until the October GDP data. StatCan hasn’t indicated whether its preliminary data fully captures the latest tariff escalation, leaving open the possibility of further weakness.

items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: One Way to Make Toronto Condos More Livable: Let Buyers Make Them Bigger
items.description:
For years, Toronto developers built condos that were an easy sell to investors, even if they weren’t ideal places to live. But with the market reckoning with a glut of “shoebox” inventory, the shortcomings of that approach are tough to ignore. Purchasers want more space from their condos; they want room to actually live.

That’s been a takeaway from One Ten Avenue Road, a boutique condominium coming up at the southern edge of Midtown Toronto, where Yorkville meets The Annex. The building will be 12 storeys with just 72 private suites, and according to Managing Partner at Sierra Building Group Jeffrey Kansun, around 45% of purchasers have chosen to merge multiple units.

This is a central feature of Sierra’s “Crafted by You” program. It’s not unusual for pre-con buyers to be able to pick their finishings and fixtures, but at One Ten Ave. purchasers are also getting a say in size and layout.

Richard Wengle Architect Inc.

“It’s been a response to the market from day one. Not everyone’s wishes fit into a box, literally and figuratively,” says Kansun. “We developed this program in response to customers — we didn’t have this idea when we started this project.”

In the first six months of presales, Sierra didn’t sell a single unit smaller than 2,500 square feet. The buyers, Kansun says, tend to be later-career homeowners who want to trade the responsibilities of a large house for something more manageable — without sacrificing so much of the space they’re used to.

That said, the need for more space is something that transcends any one type of condo buyer. A recent analysis by proptech platform Wahi found that three- and four-plus-bedroom units have held their value much better than their smaller counterparts — even with sales down across all the board. While the median sale price of a one-bedroom condo in the GTA fell 14% between the first quarter of 2020 and the first quarter of 2026 (to $480,000), two-beds rose 2% (to $630,000), three-beds rose 13% (to $700,000), and four-plus-beds rose 15% (to $715,000).

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” Wahi Economist Ryan McLaughlin said in the report. “There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them or rent them out.”

For Richard Wengle, founder of Richard Wengle Architect Inc. and the principal architect for One Ten Ave., designing for the end user has long been central to his work. Wengle’s firm has been working on projects that allow for this kind of customization since around 2011, starting with The Randall in Oakville. Since then, the firm has worked with purchasers at One Forest Hill and 89 Avenue Road (among others) to tailor layouts to their needs, including combining units to create larger, more personalized homes.

For One Ten Ave., the “typical wish-list” for units that are being combined includes things like a large kitchen and dining room, generous closet space and extra storage, and a larger patio space than you would see attached to a Toronto-area condo. These are the kinds of features that purchasers — Wengle calls them “right-sizers” — are usually giving up when moving from a home to a condo.

And then there are other requests that require a more inventive architectural approach. “One purchaser is taking one floor and part of the floor below, where they'll have a separate private section that might be for kids that come to visit,” says Wengle. “So they're not necessarily walking through space that's not being used all the time and feeling like it's wasted.”

Of course, there are limits to the program. Plumbing and mechanical stacks, elevators, corridors, and structural elements are fixed, but non-load-bearing walls can often be moved to create a layout that better suits the owner. The goal is to work within those constraints while making the most of a unit’s views, natural light, and access to outdoor space.

For now, this kind of customization remains easier to offer in the luxury market, where buyers have the budgets to purchase additional square footage and manage the costs of the architectural services and — because customized layouts require more oversight and coordination to execute — higher construction management costs for the developer. But Kansun hopes the principle behind the approach is something that will catch on in the broader pre-con condo market.

“A lot of developers stuck with very small, un-livable units, and the values have just plummeted because of it. And the unfortunate reality is that it makes sense — you can’t really sell a unit that you can’t live in,” he says. “We, as an industry, will hopefully not make the same mistake twice.”

The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just […]

The post Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The CMHC forecasts Canadian mortgage arrears will hit a 9-year high by 2027. Here is why the national housing agency might be underestimating the fallout.
items.body:
Canada’s national housing agency is bearish on real estate over the near term. The CMHC’s latest forecast shows Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) mortgage arrears climbing into 2027. The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just starting to correct.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Climbed Aggressively

The arrears rate at Canada’s banks is on an aggressive climb. The share of mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points (bps) from last year. That’s the highest rate since 2015, more than doubling from the record low less than 5 years ago. It isn’t over either.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Keep Climbing

Canadian mortgage arrears rate (90 days past due) and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The CMHC forecasts the arrears rate will continue to rise through mid-2027. They expect it to hit 0.33% by February and hold there through June 2027, the end of the forecast period. That would push arrears to the highest level since 2012.

Why The CMHC Might Be Underestimating Arrears

A closer look at the forecast reveals the agency might be underestimating the stress. The projection is primarily driven by a 58% surge in arrears in Ontario, one of 2 provinces ending the forecast at a cycle high. Slow real estate sales, a rocky job market, and a price correction are cited as the drivers. However, they’re missing a key detail—other provinces haven’t seen a correction yet.

Canadian home prices made a substantial correction after most markets slipped in 2022. However, Ontario and BC are the only provinces to see a major correction, and only the former’s drop is bigger than the national average. Despite prices across the country getting a massive lift from the low-rate boom, all but 2 remain just off record highs. Slow sales are lingering as a result of market inefficiencies that still need to correct.

These provinces don’t appear to be immune to gravity, though. Last month, prices in regions that largely resisted the correction began making near-record declines. The declines have only just started in most of the country, potentially spreading Ontario’s climate to more markets. That would prove to be a major headwind for arrears in those regions.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.

items._ogDesc: Ontario mortgage arrears are nearing 2008 levels, with Toronto leading the stress. CMHC expects arrears to keep rising through mid-2027.
items.body:
The Ontario real estate downturn is expected to worsen. Mortgage arrears in the province are approaching 2008 levels, according to the CMHC. The risk is even further amplified in Greater Toronto, especially with private lenders. The agency warns Ontario’s sharpest and most persistent surge in arrears will persist through mid-2027.

Ontario’s Real Estate Boom and Bust

Ontario was the center of Canada’s real estate bubble and now it’s the center of its bust. The low rate frenzy sent prices 64% (+$393.6k) higher between April 2020 and March 2022. Since then, prices have dropped 26.7% (-$268.8k), reversing most gains—but not all. That little nugget is important when it comes to making sense of the arrears data we’ll get to soon. But first, let’s make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to mortgage arrears.

The industry tends to frame rising arrears as a hard-hit consumer problem. In reality, households are hard hit during good times too. When someone can’t pay their mortgage, they typically try to sell. In a market boom, they sell pretty fast and feel like a genius when those profits flow in. When there’s a downturn, it takes longer to sell and not doing it fast enough means they end up in arrears. However, every property has a buyer—it’s a matter of price.

Would you rather go into arrears or lower your price? Obviously, the latter, which suggests those who don’t can’t actually do that. That’s mostly peak buyers, who in many cases see their equity wiped out entirely, and have to pay to sell. Ontario’s boom and bust is concentrated around investor-dominated Greater Toronto. CMHC doesn’t break down arrears by investors versus owner-occupiers, but the US housing crash provides some insight. Their downturn during the financial crisis is often blamed on overleveraged households, but the data shows it was an investor crash. Investors were just tapping subprime lenders to get more leverage.

Now that we have clear, let’s talk about arrears.

Ontario Mortgage Stress Builds, Private Lender Arrears Surge

Residential mortgage arrears rate at mortgage investment entities (MIEs): Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) vs Rest of Canada.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Ontario has seen a surge in mortgage arrears. The arrears rate at CBA member banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, up 52% from a year before and over 5x the low in Q2 2022. The downturn is concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario, says the CMHC.

CBA data understates the scale of the problem since it excludes roughly 1 in 5 mortgages. As previously noted, banks tend to sell or not renew underperforming or riskier loans. Those borrowers often end up at mortgage investment entities (MIEs), along with a clientele that can’t obtain traditional financing. MIEs have seen the arrears rate explode around the GTHA from 3.0% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026. These lenders represent only 1.8% of outstanding mortgage balances nationally, but their GTHA arrears rate is over three times the national rate.

“Although MIEs account for a small share of the mortgage market, GTHA MIE arrears could provide an early signal of broader mortgage market stress,” explains the CMHC.

Ontario Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Rise Through Mid-2027

Ontario CBA mortgage arrears rate and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The worst is yet to come, according to the CMHC. Even after the renewal shock, the agency expects a further erosion in credit quality in the province. They warn that the arrears rate in Ontario is expected to climb through mid-2027, with Toronto being primarily exposed.

“Ontario is projected to record the largest and most sustained increase in mortgage arrears, concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario,” warns the CMHC.

Ontario isn’t alone in the potential worsening, but high prices and a concentration of trade tensions increase sensitivity. The agency specifically cites trade tensions threatening manufacturing employment, while weak resale conditions make it harder for stressed borrowers to exit.

items.title: Award-Winning Flemingdon Park Office-Turned-Rental Makes A Case For Conversions
items.description:
Located in Toronto’s Flemingdon Park neighbourhood, e-lofts — a 15-storey office-to-residential conversion project — has won a coveted Ontario Home Builders’ Association (OHBA) award in its final months of construction.

The purpose-built rental development, which was first proposed in spring 2025, was awarded High-Rise Building of the Year at the OHBA’s 2026 Awards of Distinction Gala for “outstanding architecture, innovation, and design excellence,” according to a press release from the project’s developer, Amexon Developments. The win is significant given the low number of adaptive reuse projects in the province.

Office-to-residential conversion was an idea that picked up speed at the tail end of the pandemic, when a record-high number of office buildings were sitting vacant, and more housing was desperately needed. Why not turn those vacant offices into apartments or condos?

Turns out, it’s a bit more complex than that. In Toronto, older office buildings tend to have physical characteristics that don’t support residential layouts. For example, offices often have deep floorplates that restrict sunlight from reaching the centre of the building, or they have too few elevators or insufficient plumbing capacity — all costly deficiencies that make demolitions more attractive by comparison.

Meanwhile, red tape, like Toronto’s office replacement requirements, and a lack of municipal grants, such as Calgary’s Downtown Office Conversion Program — which offers up to $75 per square foot for qualifying adaptive re-use projects — limit the financial and logistical viability of such retrofits.

Amexon’s e-lofts, however, is one of the exceptions. “Not all buildings are suitable for conversion — this one is exceptional because it has all the right attributes to support a successful conversion into residential lofts,” says Ashling Evans, vice president of real estate at Amexon Developments. “With over 300,000 sq. ft of buildable area, infrastructure costs can be efficiently distributed across 331 units.” In comparison, smaller buildings in the 100,000–200,000 sq.-ft-range often lack the economies of scale to make conversion financially viable.

e-lofts exterior

e-lofts fitness centre

On top of sheer size, the former Flemingdon Park office building’s design made an optimal foundation for residential living. “A centrally-located elevator core allows for optimal unit planning,” says Evans. “In contrast, many office buildings have off-centre cores that limit layout flexibility and make residential conversion inefficient or impossible.”

Aside from the challenging removal of the large, heavy precast exterior walls to allow for larger residential windows, Amexon sees the building’s commercial past as an advantage.

“The adaptive reuse approach takes advantage of the building’s existing structure to deliver housing faster and more sustainably than ground-up construction,” says Evans. It has been a speedy project, with occupancy expected in summer 2027, just over two years after the initial building application was filed. “Also, the loft-style suites at e-lofts will feature 12-foot floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, exposed spiral ductwork, and structural elements for an industrial-chic aesthetic,” she adds.

Another integral aspect of the retrofit is a whole host of eco-friendly updates, including carbon-free mechanical systems that improve air quality and efficiency, green roofs and rainwater harvesting systems, and EV charging stations installed at every parking space.

e-lofts coworking space

Also available to residents will be an array of amenities. This includes a fitness centre, co-working spaces, pet daycare, and a 12,000-sq.-ft. rooftop patio with a saltwater pool, lounge areas, communal herb garden, and outdoor fitness zones.

While office-to-residential conversions haven’t taken off the way it once seemed they would, e-lofts serves as a rare example that, when physical design and financial logistics align, commercial spaces can be given new life.
